title: What Our Survey Could Not Hear
script: Narrator: [analytical] A community survey reported that eighty-two percent of residents felt safe in the central park after dark. The figure appeared in a council presentation and was repeated by a local newspaper. It looked precise enough to end the discussion.

Narrator: While reviewing the data, I noticed that the questionnaire had been distributed through a recreational app used mainly by daytime runners. Respondents needed an account and could answer only in one language. People who avoided the park at night were less likely to encounter the survey at all.
Narrator: [carefully] The percentage was not fabricated. It accurately summarised a narrow group. The mistake came when we allowed that group to stand for every resident.

Narrator: We conducted a second round through paper forms, short interviews at transport stops, and a telephone option. We asked not only whether people felt safe, but when they used the park, which routes they avoided, and what experiences informed their answer.

Narrator: [thoughtful] The new findings were more complicated. Many daytime users remained positive. Women returning from evening work described one poorly lit exit; older residents identified uneven paths; several teenagers said security staff treated them with suspicion.

Narrator: We did not combine every concern into a dramatic claim that the entire park was dangerous. Instead, the report separated user groups, time periods, observations, and limits. Personal accounts were anonymised unless explicit attribution was necessary and agreed.
Narrator: [reflective] The council improved lighting and path maintenance, then commissioned an independent review of security conduct. Follow-up data would test whether conditions changed.

Narrator: The original eighty-two percent was not useless. It answered a smaller question than the headline suggested. Responsible social research begins by asking who could respond, who had reason not to, and which experiences a convenient method was structurally unable to hear.

quiz.question: Why was the eighty-two percent figure misleading in public debate?
options: It was treated as representing people the method missed.
It had been invented by the newspaper.
It measured only path maintenance.
It used too many languages.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports it was treated as representing people the method missed.

quiz.question: What feature of the first survey restricted who could respond?
options: It was distributed through transport stops.
It relied on a daytime recreation app and one language.
It required a telephone interview.
It included only night workers.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports it relied on a daytime recreation app and one language.

quiz.question: Why were people avoiding the park less likely to appear?
options: They were prohibited from answering.
They had all moved away.
They had little reason to encounter the survey channel.
They preferred written forms.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports they had little reason to encounter the survey channel.

quiz.question: What did the second round add beyond a new percentage?
options: Proof that the park was entirely unsafe.
A single consensus among residents.
Public names for every respondent.
Context about routes, times, and experiences behind safety views.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports context about routes, times, and experiences behind safety views.

quiz.question: Why did the report avoid calling the whole park dangerous?
options: Different groups and times produced different findings.
The council rejected all criticism.
Only daytime runners mattered.
Personal accounts are never evidence.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports different groups and times produced different findings.

quiz.question: What privacy practice accompanied the new research?
options: Every interview was published in full.
Accounts were anonymised unless attribution was necessary and agreed.
Only officials could hear concerns.
Respondents were excluded from follow-up.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports accounts were anonymised unless attribution was necessary and agreed.

quiz.question: How should the original figure be used responsibly?
options: As proof of universal safety.
As a reason to cancel research.
As an answer to a narrower question about its respondents.
As an error with no value.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports as an answer to a narrower question about its respondents.

quiz.question: What does the independent security review address?
options: Whether lighting has already solved everything.
Whether residents need fewer surveys.
Whether anonymity should end.
Whether conduct concerns require separate assessment.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports whether conduct concerns require separate assessment.

quiz.question: Which research question frames the final lesson?
options: Who could respond, and who was structurally absent?
How can one headline be more dramatic?
Which group should speak for all residents?
How can accounts be made public?
quiz.explanation: The audio supports who could respond, and who was structurally absent?

quiz.question: What methodological error does the narrator identify?
options: Combining too many survey methods.
Letting a convenient sample stand for every resident.
Including time of day in questions.
Reviewing data before publication.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports letting a convenient sample stand for every resident.
